clue.text: One in fifties, ultimately unhappy, wanting company

indicators.note: Something placed 'in' another thing sits inside it, so the piece before this word goes between the letters that follow.

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty, and the plural asks for two of them
the number written out, dropped between the pair

indicators.note: Ultimately means at the very end, so only the final letter of the word beside it is taken.

parts.note: the last letter of 'unhappy'

explanation.surface: Someone in their fifties, thoroughly miserable and short of company.
explanation.walkthrough: L is the Roman fifty and the plural 'fifties' quietly asks for two of them, one on each side. 'Ultimately' is the crossword's standard word for a final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: LONELY means wanting company — being on your own and feeling the absence of anyone else.

clue.text: Crazy tenor Cyril is songwriter

indicators.note: A crazy person is out of their right mind, and letters described that way will not stay in the order handed over.

parts.note: T is the standard abbreviation for tenor on a piece of music
the rest of the fodder, seven letters taken as they stand

explanation.surface: A wild-tempered singer called Cyril who writes songs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tenor' does two jobs at once: it makes Cyril a singer in the surface and hands over the eighth letter the fodder needs to reach the enumeration.
explanation.definitionFit: A LYRICIST is a songwriter in the sense of writing a song's words; the tune is the composer's half of the job.

clue.text: No grandmother accepts bad smell — it's alien?!

parts.note: the word itself, two letters lifted straight out

indicators.note: To accept something is to take it in, so the word doing the accepting opens up and holds the next piece inside it.

parts.note: nan is the everyday British word for a grandmother
in British usage something that hums stinks — if the bins hum, they smell

explanation.surface: No grandmother will put up with a bad smell, and there is something otherworldly about this one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No' looks like the refusal that starts the sentence and it is really two letters standing on their own, which is the hardest kind of piece to see.
explanation.definitionFit: Something NON-HUMAN is alien in the adjective's core sense: belonging to another kind altogether, not one of us.

clue.text: Raid implement turned up

indicators.note: Turned up sends the letters back the way they came, and this entry runs down the grid, so they are read from the bottom upwards.

parts.note: an implement is a tool, and this is the word before it gets turned round

explanation.surface: A burglar's tool showing up after a break-in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raid' looks like the noun any sentence about a robbery would open with, and it is the verb doing the defining. LOOT and TOOL are each other backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To LOOT is to raid — both mean stripping a place of its goods by force, usually in the confusion after a fight.

clue.text: Deliberately damage bog at sea, recklessly

indicators.note: Doing something recklessly means doing it with no care for how it turns out, so the letters land wherever they fall.

parts.note: the fodder, eight letters, exactly the length wanted

explanation.surface: Wrecking a stretch of marshland out on the open water without a care.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At sea' is itself one of the commonest anagram indicators, which is why it looks like the instruction when it is really part of the fodder. 'Recklessly' at the end is the real one.
explanation.definitionFit: To SABOTAGE something is to damage it deliberately — wrecking done on purpose rather than by accident.

clue.text: Short forms of Abba's no 1 rivet Brahms and Liszt

indicators.note: Brahms and Liszt is Cockney rhyming slang for pissed, meaning drunk, and a drunk cannot keep anything in a straight line.

parts.note: the fodder, thirteen letters, with the numeral 1 taken as the letter I

explanation.surface: Abba's number one single gripping a couple of nineteenth-century composers.
explanation.walkthrough: Brahms and Liszt sitting in a clue about Abba looks like a joke about musical taste, and the numeral 1 slips into the fodder as a letter rather than a number.
explanation.definitionFit: ABBREVIATIONS are short forms — the cut-down spellings words are given so they take up less room.

clue.text: Falls over our Doberman's tail, crashing down at floor level?

indicators.note: things crashing down land in a jumbled heap, so these letters fall into a new order

parts.note: taken as written as anagram fodder
O is the cricket scorebook abbreviation for over
taken as written as anagram fodder

indicators.note: a tail is the end, so only the last letter is used

parts.note: last letter of Doberman

explanation.surface: Someone trips over the family dog's tail and comes crashing to the ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crashing down' scrambles FALLS, O (over, from cricket), OUR and N, the tail of 'Doberman's'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on all fours means crawling on hands and knees, so you are down at floor level.

clue.text: Fly from America, passing through borders of Timor-Leste

parts.note: A is a standard abbreviation for America
via means by way of, passing through somewhere on the route

indicators.note: A country's borders are its outer edges, so this takes the first and last letters of the name and nothing between them.

parts.note: the outer letters of the country's name

explanation.surface: A flight leaving the States and crossing the edges of Timor-Leste.
explanation.walkthrough: Timor-Leste counts as one hyphenated name, so its borders are the T at the very front and the E at the very back, not the edges of each half.
explanation.definitionFit: To AVIATE is to fly — the verb behind 'aviation', used of piloting an aircraft.

clue.text: Time for a snack, perhaps bite of Kissabel Eve nicked

indicators.note: A bite is a small piece taken out of something bigger, which is what is being done to the words that follow.

parts.note: the letters run on unbroken from the end of the apple's name, through the next word and into the one after

explanation.surface: Eve pinching a bite of an apple.
explanation.walkthrough: Kissabel is a red-fleshed apple variety, so the surface is Eve helping herself in the garden. Elevenses is the British mid-morning break the definition is pointing at.
explanation.definitionFit: ELEVEN o'clock is elevenses in Britain, the mid-morning snack break, so the hour stands for the snack; 'perhaps' flags one example.

clue.text: Drummer's jingle bell ball

parts.note: a jingle bell exists to ring, and the noise it makes is a ring
a ball is round, drawn as a single circle

explanation.surface: A drummer's festive kit: a jingling bell and a ball.
explanation.walkthrough: O for anything round is one of the most reliable equations in cryptics — a ball, a ring, a duck at cricket, love at tennis all come out as the same letter.
explanation.definitionFit: RINGO Starr drummed for the Beatles, so 'drummer' defines him by example — one famous holder of the job standing for the name.

clue.text: Transport provider in deep water!

definitions.meaning: reads as a bus or rail company; the setter means a single vessel that carries people and cargo
the idiom for being in serious trouble is the trap — read straight, it says the vessel travels below the surface of the sea

explanation.surface: A travel firm that has landed itself in serious trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no wordplay to take apart: both halves of the description are literally true of the same thing at once. It joins RINGO, HELP and YELLOW in the puzzle's Beatles thread.
explanation.definitionFit: A SUBMARINE is transport that operates in deep water, so both halves of the clue describe it straight — which is the whole joke.

clue.text: Are snake-shape bananas something to do with the Bard?

definitions.text: something to do with the Bard

indicators.note: Going bananas is going mad, and letters described that way will not keep the order they arrived in.

parts.note: the fodder, thirteen letters, hyphen ignored

explanation.surface: Bananas bent into snake shapes, and whether Shakespeare has anything to do with it.
explanation.walkthrough: Thirteen letters of fodder is far too many to shuffle in your head, so count them against the enumeration first — the -EAN ending is where this one starts to give way.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bard is Shakespeare, so anything SHAKESPEAREAN has to do with him: his plays, his language, his period.

clue.text: Hint endlessly and start to badger association

indicators.note: Something endless has no end, so the final letter of the word beside it comes off.

parts.note: a hint is a clue, with its last letter taken off

indicators.note: The start of a word is its opening letter, and that is all this one takes.

parts.note: the opening letter of the animal

explanation.surface: Dropping hints forever, then starting to pester someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hint' is a noun here rather than a verb, and a hint is a clue — the setter winking at the thing you are holding.
explanation.definitionFit: A CLUB is an association: a body of people formally joined together around a shared interest.

clue.text: Note setter's renown

parts.note: fa is the fourth note of the sol-fa scale
the setter is the person who wrote the puzzle, and writing about himself he is me

explanation.surface: Making a note of how well known the compiler is.
explanation.walkthrough: A setter referring to himself as ME is one of the first conventions worth owning, and the sol-fa scale supplies half the short notes in cryptics: DOH, RE, MI, FA, SO, LA, TE.
explanation.definitionFit: FAME is renown — both name the state of being widely known and talked about.

clue.text: Not finishing most recent coffee

indicators.note: not finishing means the word stops short of its final letter

parts.note: the latter is the more recent of two, the second one mentioned

explanation.surface: Someone leaves their latest coffee unfinished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not finishing' looks like a comment on the drink, but it cuts the last letter from LATTER.
explanation.definitionFit: A latte is an espresso coffee made with plenty of steamed milk.

clue.text: Ice cream, almost a ton!

definitions.meaning: the British cone with a chocolate Flake pushed into it, ordered from the van by its number
a ton is British slang for a hundred, so stopping one short of it gives the number wanted

explanation.surface: A helping of ice cream so enormous it nearly weighs a ton.
explanation.walkthrough: A ton is British slang for a hundred — of miles an hour, or of runs at cricket — so 'almost a ton' is arithmetic rather than weight.
explanation.definitionFit: A 99 is the British ice-cream cone with a Flake in it, and a ton is a hundred, so one short of a ton is NINETY-NINE.

clue.text: We heard spy let out a long breath at the beach

indicators.note: Heard reports the words by ear, so what matters is the noise they make rather than the way they are spelt.

parts.note: to spy something is to see it, and that word said aloud is written this way when it means the water
letting out a long breath is to sigh, and the past tense of it sounds identical to a word meaning edge

explanation.surface: We overheard a spy exhaling heavily down at the beach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'We heard' governs both halves of the wordplay rather than just the word next to it — a single sound indicator can cover an entire phrase, which is what makes the second half easy to miss.
explanation.definitionFit: The SEASIDE is the beach: the stretch of coast people go to in order to be beside the sea.

clue.text: God's lazy, by the sounds of it

indicators.note: By the sounds of it points at how a word is pronounced instead of how it is written down.

parts.note: lazy means idle, and that word said aloud can be written the other way

explanation.surface: A deity accused of being work-shy.
explanation.walkthrough: The two words are pronounced identically and share only two letters, which is exactly the gap a homophone clue lives in.
explanation.definitionFit: An IDOL is a god — the image or figure worshipped as one, and by extension the deity itself.

clue.text: Spar all-electric ferries running alongside

definitions.note: The definition is a participle phrase and the answer an adjective; 'running alongside' is how you would describe two parallel lines rather than a word you could swap in.

indicators.note: To ferry something is to carry it along, and these words are carrying the letters across inside them.

parts.note: the letters run straight on from inside the first word into the second, across the hyphen

explanation.surface: Electric ferries sailing side by side past a mooring spar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spar all-electric' reads as a boat's specification, and the hyphen does the camouflage: the letters carry on straight through it as though it were not there.
explanation.definitionFit: Lines that are PARALLEL run alongside one another at a constant distance and never meet.

clue.text: Spooner's displayed fish eggs for mobile exhibition?

indicators.note: Spooner swaps the opening sounds of two words, as the Reverend Spooner was said to do

parts.note: showed means displayed; its sound is written here as it is said
roe is the mass of eggs of a fish; it sounds the same as row

explanation.surface: Spooner proudly put some fish roe on show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'showed roe' has its first sounds swapped by 'Spooner's' to give 'rode show', which sounds like the answer. The question mark flags that a touring show is mobile.
explanation.definitionFit: A roadshow is a touring exhibition or entertainment that moves from town to town.

clue.text: Give me a hand — the record's skipping intro

indicators.note: skipping the intro means the opening letter is left out

parts.note: taken as written, then loses its first letter
LP, a long-playing record; the 's is just a link word for is

explanation.surface: A plea for assistance because the record keeps jumping past the start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'skipping' looks like a record jumping, but here it drops the T at the start of THE LP.
explanation.definitionFit: Help is the shout of someone needing assistance, as in asking someone to give you a hand.

clue.text: Violent storm split academy party

parts.note: something split down the middle has been torn
A is a standard abbreviation for academy
a do is British for a party or social function — a works do, a bit of a do

explanation.surface: A fierce storm breaking up a college party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Split' looks like the verb the sentence turns on, a storm breaking something up, and it is a piece of the answer instead.
explanation.definitionFit: A TORNADO is a violent storm — the whirling column of wind that tears its way across the ground.

clue.text: Hot ear, left at last, small signs of love?

parts.note: H is the letter on the hot tap
the word itself, three letters as written

indicators.note: At last points to the very end, so only the final letter of the word before it is used.

parts.note: the final letter of 'left'
S is the clothing size for small

explanation.surface: Someone complaining of a hot left ear, alongside small tokens of affection.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition wants the drawn symbol rather than the organ that beats, which is why the plural sits so oddly at the end of a sentence about one ear.
explanation.definitionFit: HEARTS are signs of love: the symbol drawn on cards and letters, so the plural names the shapes themselves.

clue.text: Energy for every season

parts.note: pep is energy, liveliness, get-up-and-go
per means for each or for every, as in miles per hour

explanation.surface: Vitality to see you through any time of year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Season' is the verb, not the noun — nothing to do with spring or autumn, everything to do with what you shake over dinner.
explanation.definitionFit: To PEPPER food is to season it, peppering being the commonest single act of seasoning there is.

clue.text: Opponent at first escaped, nevertheless eventually must yield

indicators.note: At first asks for the opening letter of each word that follows and nothing else from any of them.

parts.note: the opening letter of each of these five words, taken in order

explanation.surface: An opponent who got away at first but has to give in eventually.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At first' can reach across as many words as the enumeration needs — five of them here — which is what makes an acrostic so hard to spot inside a sentence that reads naturally.
explanation.definitionFit: An ENEMY is an opponent: the person ranged against you in a fight, a game or an argument.

clue.text: Name at the end, A N Other, concisely?

definitions.text: Name at the end, A N Other, concisely?

indicators.note: Concisely asks for the shortest possible writing of what it governs, which here means keeping initials and dropping the rest.
At the end says where a piece goes rather than which letters it is, so the one it governs is tacked on last.

parts.note: A N Other is the British team-sheet placeholder for a player not yet named; take the initial of each of its three parts
N is the standard abbreviation for name, and it is sent to the back

explanation.surface: Filling in a team sheet with the last name left blank.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole sentence is doing both jobs at once: it spells the word out of initials and describes what the word is for. A N Other is what British team sheets print when the eleventh player has not been picked.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue reads straight: ANON is the concise thing written at the end when the author is some unnamed other person.

clue.text: Group broadcasting prohibited

indicators.note: Broadcasting sends words out over the air, so you judge them by what they sound like.

parts.note: prohibited means banned, and said aloud that word can be written a letter shorter

explanation.surface: A group forbidden from going on air.
explanation.walkthrough: The doubled N disappears completely when you say it. This entry is also the last word of the Beatles album spread across the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: A BAND is a group — a set of musicians, or more generally any set of people acting together.

clue.text: Instrument to plumb loo pipe ends

indicators.note: The end of a word is its final letter, and this takes one from each of the words before it.

parts.note: the final letter of each of these four words, taken in order

explanation.surface: Sounding the depths of the lavatory pipework.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Instrument' looks like it will be a plumber's tool in a sentence about pipes, which is the whole of the misdirection — it is the woodwind.
explanation.definitionFit: An OBOE is an instrument — the double-reed woodwind — so 'instrument' defines it by example.

clue.text: Fixers, they get couples back together again?

parts.note: RE- is the prefix meaning doing a thing over again
people who put two things into a couple are pairers, and 'they' makes it plural

explanation.surface: Menders who also reunite estranged couples.
explanation.walkthrough: A hyphen is the joke: re-pairers put two things back into a couple, and run the same nine letters together without it and they mend things instead.
explanation.definitionFit: REPAIRERS are fixers: people whose job is putting broken things back into working order.

clue.text: Rebel chorister conceals burp

indicators.note: To conceal something is to keep it out of sight inside, which is where these letters are sitting.

parts.note: the letters run on from the end of the first word into the start of the second

explanation.surface: A mutinous choirboy stifling a burp.
explanation.walkthrough: A hidden answer that straddles the join between two words is far harder to see than one sitting inside a single word, and the space is what hides it.
explanation.definitionFit: To BELCH is to burp — both name the noisy release of air back up from the stomach.

clue.text: Doctor gets near police officer

indicators.note: To doctor something is to tamper with it, so the letters do not come out the way they went in.

parts.note: the fodder, eight letters, exactly the length wanted

explanation.surface: A physician drawing closer to a policeman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' is the instruction, not the man the surface puts in the room. The answer joins PEPPER, LONELY, HEARTS, CLUB and BAND — the Beatles album spread across this grid.
explanation.definitionFit: A SERGEANT is a police officer: the rank between constable and inspector in a British force.

clue.text: Cowardly, shout 'that hurts!'

parts.note: to shout is to yell
the noise you make when something hurts

explanation.surface: A cowardly yelp of pain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cowardly' looks like an adjective describing the shout that follows it, and it is the definition standing on its own at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: YELLOW means cowardly — the colour has carried that sense for well over a century, as in 'yellow-bellied'.
